title: EU, China, and Canada Launch Sweeping Retaliatory Tariffs on US Exports
description_short: EU, China, and Canada Launch Sweeping Retaliatory Tariffs on US Exports
description_medium: In 2025, Canada, the European Union and China announced retaliatory tariffs on U.S. exports after U.S. tariff measures. The supplied timeline says Canada’s 25% duties on $30 billion in goods began February 4, while China escalated to 125% on U.S. goods from April 12. The source attached to this entry is a March 4 Reuters report and does not document the later EU and China measures.
description_long: Canada, the European Union and China responded to U.S. tariffs with duties on U.S. exports during 2025. According to the supplied timeline, Canada began imposing 25% tariffs on $30 billion in U.S. goods on February 4 and added another $29.8 billion in March, covering products including steel, aluminum, computers and sports equipment. The timeline says the EU proposed duties on up to €26 billion in U.S. exports, with agricultural targets that included whiskey, soybeans, almonds and beef. It also describes China raising tariffs in stages, reaching 125% on all U.S. goods from April 12. The sequence shows how trade measures expanded across several major U.S. trading partners and multiple sectors. These were retaliatory actions, not a single coordinated tariff order: they were announced at different times and under different authorities. The supplied source link is a Reuters report from March 4, before the described April escalation and some later measures, so the specific EU and China figures need direct source citations before the whole chronology can be marked complete.
notes: The supplied synopsis contains Canada, EU and April China tariff figures, but the only linked source is Reuters dated March 4 and does not cover the complete later chronology. Additional sources are needed for the EU amount and April escalation.
proposed_correction: Keep the described measures separate by date and jurisdiction, and attach sources for the EU package and China’s April 2025 tariff changes.

title: SignalGate and Five Eyes Damage: Allies Stop Trusting US with Intelligence
description_short: SignalGate and Five Eyes Damage: Allies Stop Trusting US with Intelligence
description_medium: In March 2025, The Atlantic reported that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth shared operational details about planned strikes in Yemen in a Signal chat that included journalist Jeffrey Goldberg. The supplied record also makes separate claims about Peter Navarro and allied intelligence sharing. Its populated long description and linked Vox article do not establish that allies stopped sharing intelligence because of the Signal incident.
description_long: By March 2025, U.S. allies were restricting intelligence sharing with Washington after a series of alarming breaches. On March 24, 2025, The Atlantic revealed that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had shared classified operational details of Yemen strikes in a Signal group chat that accidentally included journalist Jeffrey Goldberg — a jaw-dropping breach that European allies said cast doubt on joint military operations. Separately, Foreign Policy reported that senior adviser Peter Navarro had pushed to expel Canada from the Five Eyes intelligence partnership. Multiple European security officials told journalists they were withholding sensitive human intelligence from the U.S., fearing Trump's history of sharing classified material with Russia. Politico reported in October 2025 that Europe had built its own independent intelligence infrastructure as a direct consequence, and that the Trump administration had abruptly halted battlefield intelligence sharing with Ukraine in March 2025.
notes: The populated long text combines the Signal chat, a separate proposal by Peter Navarro concerning Canada’s Five Eyes membership, and claims that allies withheld sensitive intelligence. The only linked Vox article concerns UK intelligence and a Caribbean operation, not the full set of claims. Preserve the long text unchanged; a source set matching the chronology and each claimed intelligence-sharing restriction is required.
proposed_correction: Keep the Signal disclosure as a distinct event and source any separate Five Eyes proposal or allied intelligence-sharing change independently.

title: 220 Lawsuits in 100 Days: Unprecedented Legal Blitz Against Trump
description_short: 220 Lawsuits in 100 Days: Unprecedented Legal Blitz Against Trump
description_medium: By April 29, 2025, the Trump administration faced at least 220 lawsuits during its first 100 days, according to ABC News. The cases challenged more than two dozen executive orders, senior-official firings and other actions. Federal judges had blocked parts of policies on immigration, military rules and diversity programs, though the administration also won some cases.
description_long: ABC News reported that Donald Trump and his administration faced at least 220 lawsuits during the first 100 days of his second term, an average of more than two per day. The suits challenged more than two dozen executive orders, the firing of 20 high-ranking officials and other executive actions. Challenges addressed a broad range of policies, including immigration measures, military guidelines and efforts to roll back diversity initiatives. By April 29, federal judges had blocked important parts of some policies, while the administration had also prevailed in other cases. The lawsuit count is a measure of legal challenges, not a count of final judgments that the administration acted unlawfully. The rapid filing pace reflected the breadth and speed of the administration’s actions and the disputes over their legal authority. The supplied reporting describes a high volume of cases at the 100-day mark; it does not establish that every challenged policy was permanently stopped or that every lawsuit had been resolved.
notes: ABC News reports at least 220 lawsuits through day 100 and identifies categories of challenged actions and blocked policies. The account distinguishes pending lawsuits and interim blocks from final legal findings.

title: Pride Flags Banned from All U.S. Embassies and Federal Sites
description_short: Pride Flags Banned from All U.S. Embassies and Federal Sites
description_medium: A 2024 federal funding bill restricted the use of its appropriated funds to fly or display certain flags over State Department facilities. NBC News reported that the provision allowed the U.S., POW/MIA, hostage, state, tribal, agency and foreign flags, and did not cover embassy grounds or offices. That provision predates the entry’s claim of a 2025 Rubio cable imposing a government-wide ban.
description_long: On January 21, 2025, Secretary of State Marco Rubio issued a 'One Flag Policy' cable to all U.S. diplomatic posts immediately prohibiting the display of any flag other than the American flag at all U.S. facilities domestic and abroad, with the only exceptions being the POW/MIA flag and the Wrongful Detainees Flag. The policy explicitly targeted pride and Black Lives Matter flags that had flown at Biden-era embassies, including the U.S. Embassy in Nassau during Pride Month 2021 and U.S. facilities in Brazil. Employees who violate the policy face disciplinary action up to and including termination or contract cancellation. The White House highlighted the policy in a news release listing actions taken in Trump's first 100 hours. The ban extended to all domestic federal buildings and official U.S. government content, effectively signaling to LGBTQ foreign nationals that American diplomatic missions would no longer publicly affirm their equality. Pride flags had first been permitted at U.S. embassies under the Obama administration and were banned during Trump's first term starting in 2019.
notes: The linked NBC article was read. It concerns a March 2024 appropriations provision, states that it did not cover embassy grounds or offices, and does not verify a January 2025 Rubio cable, a government-wide ban or the penalties asserted in the preserved long text.
proposed_correction: Preserve the original long field, but source the alleged 2025 cable and penalties separately or narrow the entry to the 2024 spending provision.

title: DOJ Directs Investigations Into George Soros-Funded Progressive Prosecutors
description_short: DOJ Directs Investigations Into George Soros-Funded Progressive Prosecutors
description_medium: In September 2025, a senior Justice Department official directed U.S. attorney’s offices in at least seven states to prepare investigations of George Soros’s Open Society Foundations. ABC News reported that the directive listed potential charges for prosecutors to consider and followed public calls by Donald Trump and JD Vance to investigate Soros. The packet also combines separate 2025 and 2026 inquiries into county prosecutors.
description_long: The supplied timeline combines three Justice Department actions involving prosecutors and organizations associated with George Soros. It says the Civil Rights Division opened a May 2025 inquiry into Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty’s policy on considering racial disparities in plea negotiations. In September, a senior official directed U.S. attorney’s offices in at least seven states to prepare investigations of the Open Society Foundations, listing potential charges including material support for terrorism, arson, wire fraud and racketeering. ABC News reported that the directive followed public calls by Trump and Vice President JD Vance to investigate Soros; the Justice Department said it investigates organizations suspected of violence or other federal crimes, while the foundation denied wrongdoing. The synopsis also describes a May 2026 civil-rights probe of Fairfax County Commonwealth’s Attorney Steve Descano over charging policy. That later inquiry is not covered by the linked September 2025 ABC report. The entries concern different subjects and dates, and the packet does not provide the later probe’s source or outcome, so the combined chronology needs additional documentation before it can be treated as a single complete account.
notes: The linked ABC News report was read and supports the September 2025 directive concerning Open Society Foundations. The supplied synopsis also combines May 2025 and May 2026 county-prosecutor inquiries; the linked source does not substantiate those separate events or the later outcome.
proposed_correction: Split the county-prosecutor inquiries from the Open Society directive, or source each date, subject and outcome separately.

title: DOGE 'Savings' Exposed as Fiction — Less Than 5% of Claimed Figures Verified
description_short: DOGE 'Savings' Exposed as Fiction — Less Than 5% of Claimed Figures Verified
description_medium: Independent analyses summarized in the supplied material found that DOGE’s claimed contract savings exceeded amounts that could be verified. One analysis of three large Health and Human Services contract cuts valued at $6.4 billion estimated about $165 million in savings; a separate review of nearly 10,100 terminations reportedly reduced a $52.8 billion claim to roughly $1.4 billion. These are different analyses and totals.
description_long: By August 2025, multiple independent analyses had systematically dismantled DOGE's cost-cutting claims. A CBS News investigation found that three of DOGE's largest claimed HHS contract cuts totaling $6.4 billion represented actual savings of roughly $165 million — about 2.6% of the stated figure. A Politico analysis of nearly 10,100 contract terminations found DOGE's claimed $52.8 billion in contract savings reduced to approximately $1.4 billion verified — less than 5%. DOGE's grand total claim of $199 billion in savings had no documentation for roughly half the amount, with budget analysts describing the figures as 'transparency theater' since DOGE was counting the full theoretical ceiling value of contracts as realized savings. Meanwhile, canceled programs included cancer research, school lunches, food bank funding, and veteran services, with a Lancet study projecting the USAID cuts alone could cause 14 million child deaths by 2030.
organization_tags: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
notes: The existing long description is populated and must remain verbatim, but it includes an unsupported claim about 14 million child deaths and combines separate totals. The only linked Washington Post report concerns an earlier review of DOGE’s claimed savings; it does not support that preserved claim or every CBS/Politico figure in the synopsis.
proposed_correction: Preserve the original long field, remove the child-death claim, and label each DOGE savings estimate with its own source, date and calculation method.

title: Family Separation 2.0: Over 100,000 US Citizen Children Separated from Detained Parents
description_short: Family Separation 2.0: Over 100,000 US Citizen Children Separated from Detained Parents
description_medium: CNN identified more than 100 U.S. citizen children who were left without a parent after immigration enforcement actions in 2025, based on verified crowdfunding campaigns, public records and interviews. The reported cases involved arrests during workplace raids, ICE check-ins and other encounters, leaving some children with relatives, friends or neighbors. The source does not support a figure of 100,000 children.
description_long: A May 2026 Brookings Institution report estimated that more than 100,000 U.S. citizen children had a parent detained since Trump's mass deportation campaign began in January 2025, out of approximately 400,000 total immigration detentions. ProPublica found at least 11,000 American children had a parent detained in just the first seven months of Trump's second term — with Trump deporting roughly four times as many mothers of American children per day as Biden. Unlike Trump's first-term border separation policy, the new separations were more dispersed and hidden, occurring inside the U.S. during interior enforcement sweeps. In a documented case, a Russian asylum-seeking couple were told to deport to Russia or have their 8-year-old son placed in a government shelter; when they refused, ICE officers in May conducted interior separation and took the boy away at Kennedy International Airport. The Trump administration stripped the word humane from its Parental Interests Directive, renaming it the Detained Parents Directive and removing guidance requiring agents to handle immigrant parents humanely.
notes: The linked CNN investigation was read. It identifies more than 100 U.S.-citizen children in reviewed cases, not 100,000; the preserved long text’s later Brookings estimate, ProPublica totals and airport case are not supported by the supplied source packet.
proposed_correction: Preserve the existing long text, but replace the unsupported 100,000 figure and later claims with figures tied to their own sources; distinguish the 2025 CNN case review from any later estimate.

title: DOJ Indicts NY AG Letitia James on Trumped-Up Fraud Charges
description_short: DOJ Indicts NY AG Letitia James on Trumped-Up Fraud Charges
description_medium: According to the supplied synopsis, a federal grand jury indicted New York Attorney General Letitia James in October 2025 on bank-fraud and false-statement charges related to a mortgage. James pleaded not guilty and called the case politically motivated. A judge dismissed the indictment in November over the prosecutor’s appointment, and later grand juries declined to re-indict her. The linked AP article concerns a separate Georgia election case.
description_long: Letitia James, the New York Attorney General who had won a landmark $454 million civil fraud judgment against Trump and his companies in 2022, became a primary target of DOJ retaliation in Trump's second term. In March 2025, FHFA Director Bill Pulte — a Trump ally — referred James to the DOJ alleging she had misrepresented information on a mortgage application. Despite a five-month investigation finding insufficient evidence to indict, Trump fired U.S. Attorney Erik Siebert in September 2025 specifically for refusing to bring charges against James and Comey. Ed Martin, Trump's special attorney and Weaponization Working Group director, sent James's attorney a letter saying he would take her resignation as an act of good faith even before any charges were filed. In October 2025, Lindsey Halligan — the same unlawfully appointed prosecutor who indicted Comey — secured a grand jury indictment against James on charges of bank fraud and making false statements. James pleaded not guilty and called the charges baseless and driven by political retribution. On November 24, 2025, the same judge who dismissed the Comey case dismissed James's indictment on the same grounds: Halligan's unlawful appointment. Subsequent federal grand juries in both Norfolk and Alexandria declined to re-indict James. The DOJ appealed. The mortgage fraud investigations of both James and Schiff were themselves investigated for potential DOJ misconduct.
notes: The linked AP article is about the Georgia election case against Trump and allies, not Letitia James. The supplied synopsis contains a detailed James chronology, but no attached source supports the mortgage referral, indictment, dismissal, later grand-jury decisions or appeal. The populated long text is preserved unchanged pending a correctly matched source.
proposed_correction: Attach a source covering James’s mortgage investigation and court proceedings, and attribute allegations and political-retaliation claims rather than treating them as findings.

title: Trump Administration Guts FOIA Infrastructure: DOGE Fires Records Officers, OPM Responds to CNN Request With Good Luck With That
description_short: Trump Administration Guts FOIA Infrastructure: DOGE Fires Records Officers, OPM Responds to CNN Request With Good Luck With That
description_medium: CNN reported in February 2025 that the Trump administration had terminated members of the Office of Personnel Management’s privacy team. In response to a CNN request for records about Elon Musk and DOGE security clearances, an official wrote, “Good luck with that, they just fired the whole privacy team.” The supplied long description adds separate FOIA, records-retention and court disputes that need their own sources.
description_long: In early 2025, DOGE's mass federal workforce reductions systematically eliminated the staff responsible for processing Freedom of Information Act requests at multiple agencies, with the Office of Personnel Management responding to a CNN FOIA request for records about Elon Musk and DOGE's security clearances with the message Good luck with that — meaning the FOIA officers had been fired. Freedom of the Press Foundation's Lauren Harper warned that agencies remained legally obligated to respond within 20 business days regardless of staffing, but that courts would find it difficult to enforce compliance without personnel in place. The Trump administration also claimed that DOGE's records were covered by the Presidential Records Act and exempt from FOIA until five years after Trump left office, arguing DOGE was a presidential advisory board rather than a federal agency — a position rejected by U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper in March 2025, though the Supreme Court blocked enforcement in June 2025. The firing of the National Archives and Records Administration head and forced resignations of senior leadership raised further alarms about preservation of government records. American Oversight and other watchdog groups filed numerous FOIA lawsuits and found systematic non-response across multiple executive agencies, documenting what Harper called an effective dismantling of the public's access to government information.
notes: The linked CNN report supports the firing of OPM privacy officials and the “Good luck with that” response. The preserved long text adds broader claims about multiple agencies, the Presidential Records Act, court orders and National Archives leadership; the supplied link does not support that full chronology, though the field itself ends as a complete sentence.
proposed_correction: Keep the original long field unchanged, but source each separate FOIA and records-retention event; distinguish the OPM privacy-team firing from wider workforce cuts.

title: Voter Suppression by Executive Fiat: Trump Orders Proof-of-Citizenship, Decertifies Voting Machines
description_short: Voter Suppression by Executive Fiat: Trump Orders Proof-of-Citizenship, Decertifies Voting Machines
description_medium: Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14248 on March 25, 2025. A federal judge later permanently barred most of its provisions, including the documentary proof-of-citizenship registration requirement, ruling that election regulation belongs to Congress and the states. PBS/AP reports the ruling on June 24, 2026. The preserved long text also claims voting-machine decertification and DOGE access to state voter files, which this source does not verify.
description_long: On March 25, 2025, Trump signed EO 14248 Preserving and Protecting the Integrity of American Elections, which the Brennan Center called an illegal attempt to take control of major parts of the nation's election systems. The order unilaterally directed the independent Election Assistance Commission to require passport-level documentation for voter registration — a show-your-papers mandate that, since only about half of Americans hold passports, would disenfranchise millions disproportionately impacting people of color, young voters, and low-income Americans. The order also directed the EAC to decertify all voting machines in 39 states within 180 days and replace them with systems that did not yet exist on the market. It granted Elon Musk's DOGE access to sensitive voter registration files from all 50 states. A federal court permanently blocked the citizenship documentation provision on October 31, 2025, finding the president lacks constitutional authority to alter election procedures.
notes: The linked PBS/AP report was read and confirms the June 24, 2026, ruling on the proof-of-citizenship provision and describes mail-ballot and funding provisions. It does not substantiate the preserved long text’s claims about decertifying voting machines in 39 states or DOGE access to all state voter files. The supplied synopsis also gives a different ruling date.
proposed_correction: Keep the citizenship requirement and court ruling tied to their documented dates; remove or separately source the claims about voting-machine decertification and DOGE access.
